newsitem.title: UK: UK rates rise seen a must to curb inflation.
newsitem.headline: UK rates rise seen a must to curb inflation.

text.p: British consumers, toasting the new year in buoyant mood, look set to be the driving force behind economic growth in 1997. But economists are warning that accelerating inflation may yet spoil the party.

With unemployment at a five-year low and consumer sentiment strengthening, they say interest rates will probably have to rise both before and after the general election, which is due by May, regardless of who wins it.
"I'm not unduly concerned about inflation, but within that context it will be tough for the government to meet its inflation target," said Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd.

The Treasury's latest compilation of independent economic forecasts in December showed underlying inflation is expected to be 3.0 percent at the end of the year, above the government target of 2.5 percent. Interest rates are seen at just over 7.0 percent compared with the present 6.0 percent.

"The most likely out-turn is an inflation rate later on this year of between 2.5 to 3.0 percent," Shepperd says. In the year to November, underlying UK inflation stuck fast at 3.3 percent, stubbornly above the government's target.
Charterhouse Tilney economist Richard Jeffrey is more pessimistic.
"In the second half of the year, inflationary pressure will build up rather more significantly than forecast," he said.
"The underlying rate will move up towards 4.0 percent by the end of the year. It's very unlikely the government will be able to fulfil its target of 2.5 percent by the end of this parliament."
Goldman Sachs senior economist David Walton expects underlying retail price inflation to rise to 3.5 percent between the second half of 1997 and the second half of 1998.
"This assumes a rise in base rates to 7.25 percent over the next six to nine months," he said.

Economists agree that sterling's meteoric rise since the summer will help to keep a lid on some of the inflationary pressures. But it will have little deflationary impact on the most buoyant area of the economy -- consumer spending.
Sterling has risen around 14 percent in trade-weighted terms since August, raising UK export prices but lowering the cost of imported raw materials and so helping to dampen inflation.
But Jeffrey said the soaring pound may even exacerbate inflationary pressures.
"If anything, against a very strong demand background, the rise in sterling might put pressure on industry to hold down export prices at the cost of domestic prices," he said.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has used sterling's rise in the past to ward off calls from the Bank of England for higher interest rates.
But Bank Governor Eddie George has warned that the quarter-point rate rise which Clarke ordered on October 30 may not be enough to bring inflation down to the government's target.

Economists agree that Clarke has the mettle to defy Conservative back-benchers worried about their re-election prospects and raise interest rates once more before the election, but they are split as to the likely timing.
Jeffrey expects Clarke to raise rates by 50 basis points at the January 15 meeting but Shepperd says the odds are stacked in favour of a rise the following month.

"The one rise we've had already shows the Chancellor is prepared to operate differently from his predecessors and is prepared to do the right thing for the economy rather than play a political game," said Shepperd.

Economists are fairly sanguine about the likelhihood of the opposition Labour party returning to power after nearly 18 years of Conservative rule -- opinion polls give Labour a commanding lead -- and they expect little disruption to monetary policy.

"A Labour government would probably not make any big shifts in the overall macroeconomic policy stance," says Michael Saunders of Salomon Brothers. "Both parties share a consensus on aiming for low inflation and fiscal restraint."
Labour leader Tony Blair has taken great pains to cultivate a new image for his party and reassure financial markets that he would pursue prudent, pro-business policies.
The opposition has yet to specify its inflation target, but economists agree it will probably keep the current aim of 2.5 percent or less.
"Most are reassured that Labour will be reasonably aggressive and will follow the policy orthodoxy established on a global basis," said Shepperd.
